Diṅnāga
or Dignāga. Bud. logician born in Sim3havaktra near Kāñcī (according to Tārānātha); studied under Vasubandhu an. lived mostly in Kaliṅga; younger contemporary of Bhartṛhari (about 30 verses of whose Vākyapadīya were taken with minor alterations in his Traikālikaparīkṣā).

-500 A. D. D.. Warder assigns him to the second half of the 4th century; 400-480 acc. to Nakamura an. 480-549 acc. to Frauwallner.
See A. K. Warder, Indian Buddhism, Delhi, 1970, p.. 447-62; Outline of Indian Philosophy. Delhi, 1971, p.. 173-90; WZKSO. V. p. 125.
Several works are ascribed to him, but the original of most of them are lost; some are preserved in Tibetan translations an. some in Chinese. [Page036-b] Vācaspatimiśra quotes some passages from Diṅnāga in his Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā. According to Mallinātha an. Dakṣiṇāvartanātha, Kālidāsa refers to him in Meghadūta, 1. 14.
Regarding his theory of Apoha, see K. Kunjunni Raja, Indian Theories of Meaning, 1969, p. 82ff.
Candrakīrti criticises his views. See J. of Indian & Bud. Studies, Tokyo,

-54, p.. 222-25 (Japanese).
A verse attributed to him in Sbhv. (3437) is found in Mahābhārata.
